units.en: oh get shifty it's shifty time today! bit shift that is here are our bit shift operations in C left shifting, right shifting and these turn into new assembly instructions shl and shr. So shift logical left we'll see a different form shift arithmetic left later on can be used with the C "<<" sign operator. Shift left takes two operands:
the first can be the source and destination which is specified in an r/mX and the second can either be cl, the least significant byte of rcx, or a single byte immediate.
Because the registers are only 64 bits long, it doesn't make sense to shift more than 64, so you can only have one byte not four bytes for instance.

Now if you even know about this C operator, you may know that it multiplies a value by 2 for each place that it's shifted to the left. So if you think about literally the number 1 and if you shift it 1 bit over then you're going to get the number 2.
If you shifted another 1 bit you're going to get the number 4.
Compilers will frequently use shifts instead of multiplies if you're multiplying by a power of 2.

Now bringing back up one of those bits I said we mostly don't care about, if you shift stuff off the left hand side of the register the sort of last bit that you shift will go into the carry flag in our rflags status register. So let's look at this example right here if we have a value 0 0 1 1 0 0 1 one and we shift it 2 bits to the left we end up with 1 1 0 0 1 1 0 0 but this bit, this last bit that was shifted off this was the first bit this was the second bit this 0 goes into the carry flag.
If we instead shift 3 bits then we get 1 0 0 1 1 0 0 0 and this was the third bit, so it's like shift 1, shift 2, shift 3 and that third bit the one that goes into the carry flag.

Then there's shr which is the ">>" operator it has the same general form as the shift left, it has two operands the first can be is the source and destination and it can be specified in an r/mX form, the second is cl the least significant byte of rcx or a 1 byte immediate. And if shifting to the left multiplies by 2,

then shifting to the right divides by 2 and the same sort of rule occurs here where whatever the last bit was that was shifted to the right it's going to go into the carry flag so here 0 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 if we shift 2 bits shift 1, shift 2, then this one right here goes into the carry flag and the rest of them are shifted down.

I should have mentioned back here on the shift logical left when you're going to the left the least significant bits are filled in with zeros and on the shift logical right when you're shifting to the right the most significant bits are filled with zeros so go ahead and take your time and wander on through this assembly to check your understanding
